summary: Gives guidance on deploying IPv6 at Internet Exchange Points, including switch fabric setup, addressing plans and organizational tasks. It advises that IPv6 should mostly be handled like IPv4. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A guide for the places where networks swap traffic, on adding the newer type of address.

questions: ipv6 at an internet exchange point
how to deploy ipv6 at an ixp
subtitle: How to add the modern address type to network meeting points

tldr.problem: Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) have deployed IPv4 for decades, but need guidance on adding IPv6 support alongside it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC shows that IPv6 deployment at IXPs is mostly like IPv4: it works at Layer 2, needs careful addressing, and requires attention to multicast, DNS, and routing policies.
tldr.outcome: IXPs can use either dual-stack LANs (one network carrying both types) or separate VLANs for IPv4 and IPv6 traffic, with each approach having trade-offs in cost and simplicity.

today: RFC 5963 is an Informational RFC that remains the primary guide for deploying IPv6 at IXPs. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What IXPs Are and Why They Need IPv6
sections.content:
An Internet Exchange Point is a physical place where many network operators connect their routers to each other and swap traffic. Most IXPs work at Layer 2 (the switching fabric level), meaning they carry data frames without looking inside them. Adopting IPv6 at an IXP sounds hard because operators worry about costs and complexity, but the RFC shows that IPv6 deployment need not differ greatly from IPv4.

The core insight is that because IXPs operate at Layer 2, IPv6 packets travel through them just as easily as IPv4 packets. The real work lies in addressing, multicast handling, reverse DNS, and operational policies.
sections.eli5: An IXP is where networks meet to swap data, like a highway interchange. Adding IPv6 is similar to adding a new lane for modern cars alongside the old one.

sections.title: Switch Fabric Configuration
sections.content:
IXP operators have two main ways to handle IPv6 traffic: either mix IPv4 and IPv6 on the same LAN (dual-stack configuration) or give IPv6 its own VLAN (separate configuration). In dual-stack mode, both types of traffic share one Ethernet broadcast domain, and operators can tell them apart using Ethertypes (0x0800 for IPv4, 0x86DD for IPv6). In independent VLAN mode, IPv4 and IPv6 traffic are logically separated, which simplifies counting which traffic is which.

The choice affects participant costs: dual-stack requires no new ports, but separate VLANs demand VLAN tagging on participant links. IPv6 links must support at least 1280 octets (the minimum allowed MTU for IPv6), which most modern Ethernet already does.
sections.eli5: You can either put both address types on the same lane (dual-stack) or give each its own lane (VLANs). Dual-stack is simpler but less organized; separate VLANs are tidier but cost more.

sections.title: Planning Addresses and Routing
sections.content:
Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) assign IPv6 address blocks—typically /48 prefixes or shorter—to IXPs for this purpose. Most IXPs use manual, static address configuration rather than automated methods, because fixed addresses let participants replace hardware without reconfiguring BGP sessions. The RFC gives four schemes for building individual addresses: encoding a participant's AS number in decimal (BCD) in the address, using hexadecimal encoding, mapping IPv4 addresses to IPv6, or using the IXP's own ID scheme.

IXPs must decide whether to advertise their LANs in global routing or keep them private. Global routing allows external monitoring but opens the door to denial-of-service attacks; private routing (using BGP no-export communities) restricts attacks but prevents external troubleshooting. External services like web pages need separate, globally routable address blocks.
sections.eli5: Each participant gets a numbered address built from their AS number or other ID. The IXP decides whether those addresses are visible worldwide (riskier but more open) or hidden inside the network (safer).

sections.title: Multicast and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
IPv6 relies on multicast for address resolution and neighbor detection (ICMPv6 Neighbor Discovery). Routers joining the IXP LAN must listen to solicited-node multicast groups (ff02:0:0:0:0:1:ff00:0000 through ff02:0:0:0:0:1:ffff:ffff) and the all-nodes group (ff02::1). IXP operators typically limit multicast, allowing only necessary address resolution and Neighbor Discovery messages while blocking unsolicited Router Advertisements (RAs) to prevent rogue routers from injecting bad configuration.

For IPv6 multicast traffic exchange (e.g., Protocol Independent Multicast), IXPs can use the same LAN as unicast traffic, the same LAN as IPv4 multicast, or a dedicated multicast LAN. Using separate multicast LANs prevents multicast packets from reaching participants that do not support it. BGP sessions for IPv6 multicast (address family indicator SAFI=2) must be configured separately if a dedicated multicast LAN is used.
sections.eli5: IPv6 uses special group addresses for routers to find each other. The IXP carefully allows the right messages while blocking bad ones that might cause trouble.

sections.title: DNS, Route Servers, and Supporting Services
sections.content:
IXP operators should populate reverse DNS zones (under ip6.arpa) with PTR records for all participant addresses, easing troubleshooting with traceroute and other tools. DNS servers themselves should be reachable over IPv6 transport for completeness. IXP route servers, which collect BGP routes for Multi-Lateral Peering Agreements or route analysis, need IPv6 support added to their BGP speakers; the RFC recommends using IPv6 as the transport for all BGP IPv6 sessions, so reachability information and data flow use the same path.

External services—traffic graphs, FTP, web pages, looking glasses, and console interfaces—should offer IPv6 access. Internal tools like provisioning systems, logging, statistics, and databases must also be checked for IPv6 support, since even if they do not handle IPv6 traffic, they may need to store and report on IPv6 addresses.
sections.eli5: Addresses should have names for troubleshooting. Tools that help operators manage and monitor the IXP need IPv6 support built in.
